title: Syphilis Treatment: Benzathine vs IV Penicillin, Neurosyphilis and the Jarisch–Herxheimer Reaction
summary: Match the penicillin preparation to the syphilis stage, see how neurosyphilis is diagnosed from CSF and serum findings, recognise the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, and know why azithromycin is not used.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 61 Hits 6 (neurosyphilis diagnosis and treatment), 7 (RPR ≥1:32 and CD4 ≤350 as neurosyphilis risk markers), 10 (Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction) and 13 (syphilis treatment; macrolide resistance) and Exam Trap 4 (benzathine for neurosyphilis), checked against the CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (Workowski 2021), Marra 2004 (abstract only; full text not open access), Butler 2017 and Stamm 2010 (both read via a page-fetch tool) and Dionne 2025. Corrections: Marra 2004 reports RPR ≥1:32 raising neurosyphilis odds 10.85-fold in HIV-uninfected and 5.98-fold in HIV-infected patients, the reverse of the reviewer’s “11× in HIV+, 6× in HIV-negative”; CDC requires neurologic signs as part of the neurosyphilis diagnosis and does not recommend CSF examination on the basis of RPR titre or CD4 count alone. Qualified: Butler 2017 argues the cytokine rise may be a result rather than the cause of the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction; Stamm 2010 does not address penicillin susceptibility of subspp. endemicum and pertenue, and macrolide resistance prevalence varies by region. Confirmed: Stamm 2010 states intramuscular benzathine does not produce treponemicidal CSF levels. Not taught: the Number Vault figures, and treatment in pregnancy or HIV beyond the risk markers.

objectives: Match the penicillin preparation, dose and duration to the stage of syphilis, including neurosyphilis.
Describe how neurosyphilis is diagnosed from CSF tests, serum tests and neurologic signs, and interpret the serum risk markers.
Recognise the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction and explain why azithromycin is not used for syphilis.

scenes.title: Three patients, one drug
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three adults with confirmed syphilis. (1) Secondary syphilis rash, given benzathine penicillin G IM; 5 hours later: fever, chills, muscle aches. (2) Serum RPR 1:64 with new confusion and a cranial nerve palsy. (3) Early syphilis, reports penicillin allergy and asks for azithromycin. Question token: “Which penicillin, and what is that fever?”

cues.text: Three adults with syphilis. The first got a benzathine penicillin injection for a secondary syphilis rash, and five hours later has fever, chills and aching muscles.
The second has a serum RPR of one to sixty-four, new confusion and a cranial nerve palsy. The third reports a penicillin allergy and asks for azithromycin.
Which penicillin does each one need, and is that fever an allergy?

props.label: Which penicillin, and what is that fever?

scenes.title: The preparation matches the stage
scenes.altText: Schematic treatment cards from the CDC 2021 STI guidelines. Parenteral penicillin G is preferred for every stage; preparation, dose and duration depend on stage. Primary, secondary and early latent syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose. Late latent: 3 weekly doses of 2.4 million units (7.2 million units total). Sequestered sites such as the CNS and aqueous humour are poorly reached by certain penicillin forms; a 2010 review notes IM benzathine gives weeks of treponemicidal blood levels but not treponemicidal CSF levels. Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units per day IV (3–4 million units every 4 hours or continuous infusion) for 10–14 days. A 2010 review: no documented penicillin resistance in T. pallidum.

cues.text: Parenteral penicillin G is the preferred drug for every stage of syphilis. What changes is the preparation, the dose and the duration.
Primary, secondary and early latent syphilis: one intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G, two point four million units. Late latent syphilis: the same dose weekly for three weeks.

The nervous system and the eye are sequestered sites that some penicillin forms reach poorly; benzathine does not give treponemicidal CSF levels. So neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis get aqueous crystalline penicillin G, eighteen to twenty-four million units a day intravenously, for ten to fourteen days.
And the drug still works: a 2010 review found no documented penicillin resistance in Treponema pallidum.

props.label: Parenteral penicillin G for every stage

scenes.title: Diagnosing neurosyphilis
scenes.altText: CNS involvement can occur at any stage. CSF examination when there are neurologic signs (cognitive dysfunction, motor or sensory deficits, cranial nerve palsies, meningitis or stroke). Diagnosis combines CSF tests (cell count, protein, CSF-VDRL) with reactive serum treponemal and nontreponemal tests and neurologic signs; no single test is enough. CSF-VDRL: highly specific, insensitive; reactive (without blood contamination) in a patient with neurologic signs = diagnostic. CSF FTA-ABS: sensitive, less specific; negative makes neurosyphilis highly unlikely. CSF abnormalities are common in early syphilis and of unknown significance without neurologic signs. Risk card (Marra 2004, abstract): RPR ≥1:32 raised the odds of neurosyphilis 10.85-fold in HIV-uninfected and 5.98-fold in HIV-infected patients; CD4 ≤350/µL raised them 3.10-fold in HIV-infected patients. Caveat token (CDC 2021): CSF examination and neurosyphilis treatment based on laboratory abnormalities alone have not been associated with better outcomes without neurologic signs.

cues.text: Treponemes can reach the nervous system at any stage. When a patient with syphilis has neurologic signs, such as a cranial nerve palsy, cognitive dysfunction, or signs of meningitis or stroke, the cerebrospinal fluid is examined.

No single test settles it. Diagnosis combines CSF cell count, protein and CSF-VDRL with reactive serum tests and neurologic signs. CSF-VDRL is highly specific but insensitive: reactive, without blood contamination, in a patient with neurologic signs, it is diagnostic.
CSF FTA-ABS is the opposite: sensitive but less specific, so a negative result makes neurosyphilis highly unlikely. And CSF abnormalities are common in early syphilis even without neurologic signs.

Serum markers flag risk. In one study, an RPR of one to thirty-two or more raised the odds about eleven-fold without HIV and six-fold with HIV; a CD4 of 350 or less, about three-fold with HIV. But CDC notes that acting on these markers without neurologic signs has not improved outcomes.

props.label: No neuro signs: markers alone, no proven benefit

scenes.title: After the injection
scenes.altText: Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction card (CDC 2021): acute febrile reaction with headache and myalgia within the first 24 hours of any syphilis therapy; a reaction to treatment, not penicillin allergy; most frequent in early syphilis; antipyretics ease symptoms but are not proven to prevent it. Trial card (Dionne 2025): 59 of 249 adults (23.7%) treated for early syphilis had symptoms; median onset 4.9 hours. Butler 2017: also seen in Lyme disease, leptospirosis and relapsing fever; TNF, IL-6 and IL-8 rise, but the review argues the rise may follow rather than cause the reaction. Macrolide card: T. pallidum 23S rRNA mutations (A2058G, A2059G) cause macrolide resistance; CDC: azithromycin should not be used for syphilis. Hook answers: (1) Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, not allergy; (2) CSF exam, then IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G if neurosyphilis; (3) no azithromycin; penicillin-allergy pathway per guideline.

cues.text: Within the first twenty-four hours of any syphilis treatment, an acute febrile reaction with headache and aching muscles can appear. This is the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction: a reaction to treatment, not an allergy to penicillin.
It is most frequent in early syphilis. In one trial, about a quarter of adults treated for early syphilis had symptoms, with a median onset just under five hours.
It also follows treatment of Lyme disease, leptospirosis and relapsing fever. TNF, interleukin six and interleukin eight rise, though whether they cause it is still debated.
Azithromycin is a different story. Point mutations in the 23S ribosomal RNA genes make Treponema pallidum macrolide-resistant, so azithromycin should not be used.

Back to the hook: patient one has a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction. Patient two needs a CSF exam and, if neurosyphilis is confirmed, intravenous aqueous penicillin. Patient three should not get azithromycin.

props.label: TNF, IL-6, IL-8 rise: cause or effect?

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 2 CSF, then IV aqueous pen G

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Treat neurosyphilis with benzathine penicillin G” (✓ IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day for 10–14 days); “Fever after the first dose = penicillin allergy” (✓ Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, a reaction to treatment); “Azithromycin is a fine alternative” (✓ 23S rRNA macrolide resistance; CDC says do not use).

cues.text: Trap one: treat neurosyphilis with benzathine penicillin. No: neurosyphilis needs intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G for ten to fourteen days.
Trap two: fever after the first dose means penicillin allergy. No: that is the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, a reaction to treatment.
Trap three: azithromycin is a fine alternative. No: 23S ribosomal RNA mutations cause macrolide resistance, and the CDC says not to use it.

props.title: ✗ “Benzathine for neurosyphilis.”
lines: ✓ IV aqueous crystalline pen G, 10–14 days

scenes.title: Depot for the body, drip for the brain
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Depot for the body, drip for the brain.” Benzathine is a slow intramuscular depot for early (and, weekly, late latent) syphilis; neurosyphilis gets an intravenous drip of aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10–14 days. Tokens: depot = benzathine IM · drip = aqueous IV. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: depot for the body, drip for the brain. Benzathine is a slow intramuscular depot for early syphilis; the brain gets an intravenous drip of aqueous crystalline penicillin for ten to fourteen days.

Where it breaks: the eye and ear also get the brain regimen; an intramuscular alternative, procaine penicillin plus probenecid, exists for neurosyphilis; and late latent syphilis needs three weekly depot doses, not one.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Early syphilis: benzathine IM × 1 · neurosyphilis: aqueous pen G IV 10–14 days”, “Fever within 24 h = Jarisch–Herxheimer, not allergy · no azithromycin”.

cues.text: Treat early syphilis with one intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin but neurosyphilis with 10 to 14 days of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin, and recognise a fever within 24 hours of treatment as the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction rather than penicillin allergy.

props.label: Early: benzathine IM × 1 · Neuro: aqueous pen G IV 10–14 d
Fever < 24 h = Jarisch–Herxheimer, not allergy · no azithromycin

explanation.what: Plain language: penicillin cures syphilis, but the form matters. A long-acting injection in the muscle works for early disease; when the infection reaches the brain, eye or ear, the patient needs high-dose penicillin through a vein for up to two weeks. Some people (about a quarter in one trial) feel feverish and achy within hours of the first dose; that is a reaction to the treatment, not an allergy. Scientific terms: benzathine penicillin G, aqueous crystalline penicillin G, procaine penicillin plus probenecid, sequestered sites, CSF-VDRL, CSF FTA-ABS, pleocytosis, Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, 23S rRNA A2058G/A2059G mutation, macrolide resistance.
explanation.why: The CNS and aqueous humour are sequestered sites poorly reached by certain penicillin forms, so neurologic, ocular and otic syphilis need the intravenous regimen; a 2010 review notes intramuscular benzathine gives weeks of treponemicidal blood levels but does not produce treponemicidal CSF levels. Neurosyphilis diagnosis needs several findings together because CSF-VDRL is insensitive and CSF abnormalities are common in early syphilis without neurologic disease. Single point mutations in the 23S rRNA genes are enough for macrolide resistance, whereas no penicillin resistance had been documented as of a 2010 review, which expects it would need a multistep mutational process.
explanation.measure: Primary, secondary, early latent: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once. Late latent: 2.4 million units IM weekly × 3 (7.2 million units). Neurosyphilis, ocular, otic: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV (3–4 million units every 4 h or continuous infusion) for 10–14 days; alternative procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM daily plus probenecid 500 mg orally 4 times/day for 10–14 days. CSF-VDRL reactive (no blood contamination) + neurologic signs = diagnostic. Marra 2004: RPR ≥1:32 OR 10.85 (HIV-uninfected), 5.98 (HIV-infected); CD4 ≤350/µL OR 3.10 (HIV-infected). Jarisch–Herxheimer: within 24 h; 23.7% in one early-syphilis trial, median onset 4.9 h.
explanation.differs: Benzathine IM depot (early and latent syphilis) vs aqueous crystalline IV (neurologic, ocular, otic); CSF-VDRL (specific, insensitive) vs CSF FTA-ABS (sensitive, less specific); Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (reaction to treatment) vs penicillin allergy; macrolide resistance (documented) vs penicillin resistance (none documented).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the regimen for neurosyphilis, name the fever a few hours after the first dose, pick the diagnostic CSF finding, or explain why azithromycin is avoided.

mnemonic.limitation: Ocular and otic syphilis also get the brain regimen; an intramuscular procaine-plus-probenecid alternative exists for neurosyphilis; late latent syphilis needs three weekly depot doses.

Risk-marker odds ratios come from one study; the Jarisch–Herxheimer frequency comes from one trial.
takeaway: Treat early syphilis with one intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin but neurosyphilis with 10 to 14 days of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin, and recognise a fever within 24 hours of treatment as the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction rather than penicillin allergy.

questions.stem: A patient with syphilis and new cranial nerve palsy has a reactive CSF-VDRL. According to the CDC 2021 guidelines, which regimen is recommended?

options.text: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV for 10–14 days
options.rationale: Correct. This is the recommended neurosyphilis regimen.

options.text: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. This treats primary, secondary and early latent syphilis; benzathine does not produce treponemicidal CSF levels, so it is not used for neurosyphilis.
Incorrect. Macrolide resistance from 23S rRNA mutations and treatment failures mean azithromycin should not be used.

options.text: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the late latent regimen; it may follow a neurosyphilis course but does not replace it.

questions.stem: Five hours after benzathine penicillin G for secondary syphilis, a patient develops fever, headache and myalgia. What is the most likely explanation?

options.rationale: Correct. An acute febrile reaction within 24 hours of syphilis therapy, most frequent in early syphilis, is a reaction to treatment.
Incorrect. CDC states the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction is not an allergic reaction to penicillin.

options.text: Treatment failure from penicillin-resistant T. pallidum
options.rationale: Incorrect. A 2010 review found no documented penicillin resistance in T. pallidum, and treatment failure would not show up as fever within hours.
Incorrect. Fever with headache and myalgia hours after a dose fits the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, not new neurologic disease.

questions.stem: In a patient with neurologic signs and reactive serum syphilis tests, which CSF finding is considered diagnostic of neurosyphilis?

options.rationale: Correct. CSF-VDRL is highly specific; a reactive result in a patient with neurologic signs is diagnostic.
Incorrect. CSF FTA-ABS is sensitive but less specific; its value is that a negative result makes neurosyphilis unlikely.
Incorrect. CSF-VDRL is insensitive, so a nonreactive result does not exclude neurosyphilis.
Incorrect. A high serum RPR raises the odds of neurosyphilis but is a serum risk marker, not a CSF diagnosis.

claims.text: Parenteral penicillin G for all stages; benzathine regimens for early and late latent syphilis; aqueous crystalline IV regimen and procaine-probenecid alternative for neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis; sequestered sites.
Neurosyphilis diagnosis: neurologic signs plus CSF tests and reactive serology; CSF-VDRL specific/insensitive; CSF FTA-ABS sensitive/less specific; CSF abnormalities common in early syphilis.
RPR ≥1:32 odds ratios 10.85 (HIV-uninfected) and 5.98 (HIV-infected); CD4 ≤350 odds ratio 3.10 (HIV-infected).

Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction: febrile reaction within 24 h, not allergy, most frequent in early syphilis; 23.7% and median onset 4.9 h in one trial; also after Lyme, leptospirosis, relapsing fever treatment; TNF, IL-6, IL-8 rise with debated causality.

Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G gives weeks of treponemicidal blood levels but does not produce treponemicidal CSF levels; CDC: CNS and aqueous humour are sequestered sites poorly accessed by certain penicillin forms.
No documented penicillin resistance (as of 2010); 23S rRNA point mutations cause macrolide resistance; azithromycin should not be used.
All T. pallidum subspecies uniformly penicillin-susceptible; macrolide resistance “rampant”; Number Vault spirochete figures.
claims.note: Not taught as stated. Stamm 2010 names subspp. endemicum and pertenue but does not address their penicillin susceptibility, and shows macrolide resistance varying widely by region.

claims.text: “Depot for the body, drip for the brain.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 61 Hit 7 (and the Number Vault) give RPR ≥1:32 neurosyphilis risk as 11× in HIV+ and 6× in HIV-negative patients. Marra 2004 reports the reverse: 10.85-fold in HIV-uninfected and 5.98-fold in HIV-infected subjects. CDC 2021 also states that CSF examination followed by neurosyphilis treatment on the basis of laboratory abnormalities has not been associated with improved clinical outcomes without neurologic signs (register flag rv-neurosyphilis-rpr-odds).

Ch. 61 Hit 6 defines neurosyphilis as a positive serum treponemal test plus positive CSF VDRL or pleocytosis/elevated protein. CDC 2021 makes neurologic signs and symptoms part of the diagnosis, notes CSF abnormalities are common in early syphilis without clinical significance, and considers a reactive CSF-VDRL diagnostic only in a patient with neurologic signs (register flag rv-neurosyphilis-dx-signs).

Ch. 61 Hit 10 attributes the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction to a TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8 cytokine storm. Butler 2017 reports these cytokines rise but argues the rise appears to result from, rather than cause, the reaction, implicating spirochetal lipoproteins (register flag rv-jhr-cytokine-causality).

Ch. 61 Hit 13 says all T. pallidum subspecies are uniformly penicillin-susceptible and macrolide resistance is rampant. Stamm 2010 reports no documented penicillin resistance in T. pallidum but does not address the penicillin susceptibility of subspp. endemicum and pertenue, and macrolide-resistance prevalence varies widely by region (register flag rv-tpallidum-resistance-scope).
Regimens and CSF criteria taught are US CDC 2021 recommendations; Philippine and other national guidelines are not covered, and MTLE candidates should check local guidance.
